questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Textual and Tabular Presentation' refers to.
questions.a: Data can be presented in text, where figures are woven into sentences and comparisons stay hard to grasp, or in tables -- the master device of presentation, with stub for the rows, caption for the columns, and cells holding the figures in compact, comparable form.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Textual and Tabular Presentation'.
questions.a: Prose hides figures, tables display them -- stub, caption and body make data speak at a glance.

concepts.title: Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts

questions.q: Using the method 'Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts', work with: component = 400, total = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of angle.

Take the relation taught for 'Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts' and work with: component = 80, total = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of angle.
Explain in your own words what 'Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts' refers to.
questions.a: Diagrams translate figures into pictures. Bar diagrams of one dimension compare magnitudes through length -- simple, multiple, component and percentage bars; the pie chart slices a circle so that each component's angle shows its share of a total of 360 degrees.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Diagrammatic Presentation: Bar Diagrams and Pie Charts'.
questions.a: Lengths compare, circles share -- bar diagrams for magnitudes, pie charts for parts of a whole.

concepts.title: Frequency Diagrams: Histogram, Polygon and Ogive

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Frequency Diagrams: Histogram, Polygon and Ogive' refers to.
questions.a: Frequency distributions get their own pictures: the histogram joins adjacent rectangles over class intervals; the frequency polygon connects mid-points of the rectangles; and the ogive plots cumulative frequencies, rising to the total. These graphs reveal the shape of a distribution at sight.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Frequency Diagrams: Histogram, Polygon and Ogive'.
questions.a: Rectangles for classes, lines for mid-points, curves for cumulative counts -- the distribution's silhouette in three graphs.
